## The incident

The European System of National Accounts, ESA95, requires that illegal transactions "to which all units involved consent" be included in GDP. Section 1.13 applies across Europe; member states' gross national income is used to calculate EU budget contributions. In 2012 the EU audited national accounting methods across all members. By 2014 member states had to implement improvements.

In May 2014 ONS published its method. For prostitution: P × C × 52. P is the number of prostitutes. C is weekly clients per prostitute. 52 is weeks per year. The Eaves charity estimated approximately 7,000 off-street prostitutes in London in 2004 by telephoning advertisements; adding Metropolitan Police street counts gave roughly 58,000 for the whole country. Clients per week came from "a Netherlands assumption" of 20, 25, or 30 per week (which figure was chosen is not stated). Price was £55 in 2004, sourced from Punternet; a footnote references Wikipedia.

Four assumptions are listed. One: "the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption." For drugs, the article states: "We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." Also: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." The words "probably false" appear 3 times in the assumptions table.

ONS publishes the series from 1985 onwards. No direct observations exist for 1985 to 2003. The series is calculated backward by scaling the 2004 point estimate against population growth and price inflation. In 2020 the series fell 31%, from £5,993m in 2019 to £4,130m. ONS has published no explanation for this movement.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published the method as a peer-reviewed article, naming the assumptions and flagging their limitations.

## The bit continues

In 2016 ONS refined the estimate. It reduced prostitution expenditure by applying a factor for time off work. Statistics Netherlands had estimated that sex workers take 12 weeks of holiday per year; ONS applied the same adjustment to UK figures.

The effect appears in 2010 data. An ONS FOI response from November 2015 stated that prostitution was £5.6bn in 2010. The current MNC8 series lists 2010 as £4,370m. That ratio, 0.78, matches the working-week ratio: 40/52 = 0.77. The change aligns with the holiday factor, though ONS has not confirmed this accounts for the entire difference.

The series is still published. The last release was 31 October 2025.

The audit identified areas for improvement, to be addressed by 2014. One: the European System of Accounts required member states to include illegal activities in GDP when "all units involved consent". Prostitution and drugs qualified.

ONS published its method in May 2014. Authors: Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew. The executive summary: "significant limitations in the availability of data ... requires a number of assumptions on which the estimates are, therefore, partly based. This applies especially to the estimates of prostitution activity."

C: "Following a Netherlands assumption with some research support", 20, 25 or 30. Price: £55 in 2004, from "an estimate from Punternet supported by a 2004 journal article", varied by the consumer price index for personal services. Footnote 12 for Punternet: "http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punternet".

Time series: none. Assumption 1: "the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption ... It is necessary because we have no time series data for the number of prostitutes."

## Who lied

Nobody. The article lists its assumptions in Table 3. On drugs: "We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." On cannabis: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On government consumption: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

"Probably false" appears 3 times in the article. "Arbitrary" appears twice.

The employment assumption: "There is no employment in prostitution; all prostitutes and pimps are self-employed. This is a controversial assumption."

Patterson, ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, in October 2014: "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP."

## The incident

National accounts in the EU must include illegal activity. ESA95 section 1.13 says consensual illegal transactions "are included within the production boundary", and ONS notes this is unchanged in its successor: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA 2010." The reason to care: GNI "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and a 2012 audit identified areas for Member States to address by 2014.

So in 2014 ONS added drugs and prostitution to UK GDP. Peter Patterson, then Deputy Chief Economic Adviser, wrote on a gov.uk blog that "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP."

The method is the exhibit. There is no survey, so ONS built the number from assumptions. Prostitution volume is "P*C*52". For the headcount, a charity's 2004 London estimate of "approx 7000 off-street prostitutes" and a Metropolitan Police count of "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time" were added and "scaling up by UK population ... gives c. 58,000 prostitutes in the whole country." Clients per week came from "a Netherlands assumption". The price came from Punternet, footnoted to a Wikipedia page.

"As there is no time series, we vary the point estimates in time using the male population." ONS calls that "a weak assumption".

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS flagged every weakness itself. The drugs table reads: "This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it." On cannabis: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On public spending: "The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." The phrase "probably false" appears 3 times.

The series is still published. The latest release is 31 October 2025.

In Blue Book 2016 ONS refined the estimate, reducing it "by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

The figures moved. A November 2015 FOI reply gives 2010 prostitution as "£5.6bn (current prices), which is 0.4% of GDP". Today's MNC8 series gives 2010 as £4,370m. ## The incident

In 2014 the Office for National Statistics added illegal drugs and prostitution to UK GDP. The change followed a 2012 EU audit: gross national income "is used in the calculation of a Member State's contribution to the EU budget", and member states had to align their methods by 2014. The underlying rule was not new. The European System of National Accounts 1995, section 1.13, already put illegal transactions "to which all units involved consent" inside the production boundary, and ONS's own footnote confirms the successor rule, ESA 2010, is identical: "There are no changes in this area between ESA95 and ESA10."

The article that announced the change, by Joshua Abramsky and Steve Drew, published the method and its weaknesses in the same document. On cannabis: "We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption." On government spending: "government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs." On prostitution: "there is no time series", so a formula of prostitutes times clients times 52 weeks runs on a single 2004 estimate, scaled since by the male population. That estimate combined a charity's count of "approx 7000 off-street prostitutes in London", made by phoning numbers advertised in various media, with the Metropolitan Police's count of "115 prostitutes on the street at any one time", scaled to a UK total of "c. 58,000". The price per client, £55 in 2004, came from Punternet, footnoted to a Wikipedia page.

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published its own weak points beside its numbers. The 2014 article uses "probably false" 3 times and "arbitrary" twice about its own assumptions, including the claim that prostitute numbers "has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population", which it calls "a weak assumption". Treating all prostitutes and pimps as self-employed is called "a controversial assumption".

Peter Patterson, ONS's deputy chief economic adviser, wrote in an October 2014 blog that illegal activities and R&D together raised GDP "by around £50 billion a year, some 4%", and that the inclusion is "legally mandated through the European System of Accounts 2010". ONS's own 2014 article says otherwise about the rule's history: nothing changed between ESA95 and ESA 2010.

## The bit continues

Blue Book 2016 added a further adjustment: "allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution... to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes." Statistics Netherlands had put the total at "12 weeks per year"; ONS applied the same factor to the UK.

Two publications give two figures for the same year. A November 2015 FOI response puts 2010 prostitution in GDP at £5.6bn. The MNC8 series today puts the same year at £4,370m. 4,370 divided by 5,600 is 0.78; 40 of 52 working weeks is 0.77. That arithmetic is this site's, not ONS's; ONS does not say the holiday accounts for the whole gap.

The series is still published. Last release: 31 October 2025. 2024 figure: £6,431m.

## The incident

A 2012 EU audit required Member States to address illegal activities by 2014. The European System of Accounts 1995 section 1.13 states that illegal transactions to which all units involved consent are included within the production boundary. GNI is used to calculate EU budget contributions. Comparability required all countries to include it.

In May 2014 ONS published its method for including illegal drugs and prostitution in UK GDP. The executive summary noted "significant limitations in the availability of data" and that the estimates were "partly based" on assumptions, "especially" for prostitution. The article stated "there is no time series" for the number of prostitutes.

The method: multiply prostitutes by clients per week by 52. Number of prostitutes: a 2004 charity called advertised numbers and asked how many prostitutes were at each location, finding 7,000 off-street in London. The Metropolitan Police counted 115 on-street. Scaled to the UK: c. 58,000. Clients per week: "Following a Netherlands assumption", ONS calculated estimates based on 20, 25 and 30. Price: £55 in 2004, from Punternet. Footnote 12 cited Wikipedia.

Because there was no time series, ONS varied the point estimate by the male population. Assumption 1: "the number of prostitutes has the same pattern through time as the 16+ male population. This is a weak assumption."

## Who lied

Nobody. ONS published a table of assumptions. 3 are reproduced verbatim here.

"We assume that the purity-adjusted amount of drugs consumed by the average user remains constant over time. This assumption is probably false, but we have no data to challenge it."

"We assume that half of cannabis sold in the UK is imported and half home-grown. This is an arbitrary assumption."

"The government final consumption expenditure assumption is reasonable because government units are very unlikely to spend money on illegal drugs."

The word "arbitrary" appears twice in the article; "probably false" appears 3 times.

In October 2014 the ONS Deputy Chief Economic Adviser published "Sex, Drugs and GDP" on the Civil Service Quarterly blog. "ONS desk research (please note the italics for emphasis!) into the numbers of prostitutes and the price of drugs yielded the result that spending on these illegal activities in the UK contributes up to £10 billion a year to the level of GDP." The italics were his.

## The bit continues

An FOI response in November 2015 gave the 2010 prostitution figure as £5.6bn. The Blue Book 2016 revisions article described a refinement: "allowance was made to reduce the estimates made for prostitution in household final consumption expenditure by a factor to reflect the holiday taken by prostitutes. Statistics Netherlands have estimated the total holidays to be 12 weeks per year and the same factor has been applied to the UK estimates."

The time series MNC8, last released 31 October 2025, gives prostitution in 2010 as £4,370m. The series runs from 1985 to 2024. In 2019 it stood at £5,993m. In 2020 it fell 31% to £4,130m. By 2022 it had recovered to £6,142m. The method says there is no time series. The chart plots the assumptions.
